content: Rudbeckia hirta, commonly known as Black-eyed Susan, Blackiehead, Brown Betty, Brown Daisy, Brown-eyed Susan, Gloriosa Daisy, Golden Jerusalem, Poorland Daisy, Yellow Daisy, or Yellow Ox-eye Daisy, is a flowering plant belonging to the family Asteraceae. It is an upright plant that is typically annual but can sometimes be biennial or perennial. This species is native to most regions of North America and is one of several plants referred to by the common name Black-eyed Susan, which also features purple coloration on the sides. The plant can grow to a height of 1 to 2 meters. Its leaves are arranged alternately, primarily basal, and measure between 20 and 75 cm in length. These leaves are covered with coarse hair. Rudbeckia hirta blooms from June to August, producing inflorescences that are 10 to 15 cm in diameter, though some cultivars can reach up to 30 cm. The flowers consist of yellow ray florets encircling a brown, domed center composed of disc florets. There are four recognized varieties of Rudbeckia hirta: 1. Rudbeckia hirta var. angustifolia: Found in the southeastern United States, from South Carolina to Texas. 2. Rudbeckia hirta var. floridana: Endemic to Florida. 3. Rudbeckia hirta var. hirta: Found in the northeastern United States, from Maine to Alabama. 4. Rudbeckia hirta var. pulcherrima: Widespread across most of North America, from Newfoundland to British Columbia, and south to Alabama and New Mexico. It has also been naturalized in regions from Washington to California. Symbolism and Uses In 1918, Black-eyed Susan was designated as the state floral emblem of Maryland. Numerous cultivars have been developed for garden use, with popular varieties including 'Double Gold,' 'Indian Summer,' and 'Marmalade.' The roots of Rudbeckia hirta, though not its seed heads, can be used similarly to the related plant Echinacea purpurea. The plant has astringent properties and can be prepared as a warm infusion for washing sores and swellings. The Ojibwe people traditionally used it as a poultice for snake bites and to create an infusion for treating colds and intestinal worms in children. Additionally, the plant has diuretic properties and was utilized by the Menominee and Potawatomi tribes. Juice extracted from the roots was historically used as ear drops to alleviate earaches. The plant contains anthocyanins, which are pigments with potential health benefits. Inflorescence and Involucral Bracts The inflorescence and involucral bracts of Rudbeckia hirta are notable features. The cultivar 'Indian Summer' is particularly well-known and has been observed in regions such as southern Maine.
